name: Abeka
line: Abeka teaches a set daily lesson in a fixed order. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Abeka: Abeka teaches daily lessons in a fixed order, graded by the adult. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Abeka teaches math in daily lessons, on video with textbooks, in a fixed order that is the same for every learner in a grade. The adult grades the work against answer keys [2][3][8]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Abeka measures progress with quizzes, tests and exams [2]. In the video-only option the adult grades them against answer keys [3][8]. In grades 9 to 12 of the accredited option Abeka grades the exams [3].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Abeka the unit is the day's lesson: a master teacher on video, then written work in the textbook [2][4]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [13].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each problem AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In Abeka the adult checks written work against answer keys, which come with the quizzes and tests [3][4][8]. Abeka staff review the grades a parent gives and may change them [6]. We found no description of what happens at the moment a learner answers. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest effect, as an average across ages and subjects [12].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. In Abeka every learner in a grade gets the same lessons in the same order, and each day brings the next one. A grade is designed to take ten months [2].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In Abeka, review is part of the set lessons: its grade 12 page describes lessons with reviews and drills [7]. We found no schedule for when a skill comes back. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [11].

reasons.title: Paper made for one learner
reasons.body: AMP makes printable workbooks for each learner from that learner's own record, with worked answer keys, and work done on paper counts. Abeka's textbooks, workbooks, and quiz and test books come as a kit for each grade, the same for every learner in it [8].

rows.range: Abeka Academy runs from K4 through grade 12. Grade 12 math is Precalculus or an elective [5][7].
rows.start: No placement test found in the pages we read. Books come as a kit for each grade [8].
rows.teaching: A daily lesson from a master teacher on video, then written work in the textbook [2][4].
rows.next: The next lesson in a fixed order, the same for every learner in the grade. A grade is designed to take ten months [2].
rows.mastery: Progress is measured by quizzes, tests and exams [2]. No rule for when a skill counts as learned found in the pages we read.
rows.review: Reviews and drills within the set lessons [7].
rows.print: Print is the core: textbooks, teacher editions, quiz and test books and answer keys, in a kit for each grade [8].
rows.adult: Sets the calendar, supervises, and in the video-only option grades quizzes and tests against answer keys. In the accredited option, submits work and progress reports each grading period [2][3].
rows.reports: A dashboard for the calendar and assigned work [2]. The accredited option adds report cards, a transcript and a diploma [3].
rows.evidence: None found. We found no Evidence for ESSA entry. The What Works Clearinghouse's one Abeka report, on early childhood (2005), found no qualifying studies [9][10].

theirs: Abeka is a Christian publisher; its site is copyrighted by Pensacola Christian College [1]. It publishes curriculum taught from a Christian perspective, for homeschool families and Christian schools [1]. Abeka Academy runs from K4 through grade 12, and grade 12 offers Precalculus or a math elective [5][7].

Families use it in two ways. Parent Led kits hold a grade's textbooks, teacher editions, quiz and test books and answer keys [8]. Abeka Academy adds daily video lessons from master teachers, in a fixed order, with a grade designed to take ten months [2][4]. In the video-only option the adult grades the work against the keys [3]. In the accredited option, Abeka keeps the records [3]. Abeka staff review the grades a parent gives [6].
credit: A master teacher on video teaches each lesson, with a video manual to guide the adult [2][5].
A complete course for each grade: lessons, practice, quizzes, tests and answer keys in one set [8].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Abeka's math on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][9][10]. The Clearinghouse's only Abeka report, from 2005, covers early childhood education, not math, and found no studies that met its standards [10].
Abeka's home page says its textbooks are "tested in the real world" and cites no study [1]. Abeka Academy is accredited by MSA CESS and FACCS, and the pages we read give no outcome data with it [3].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains averaged 0.49, the correct answer alone 0.32, and right or wrong only 0.05; these are average effects across ages and subjects [12]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [11]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want a teacher on video to teach each day's lesson, in a set order through the grade.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer checked and followed by the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want math checked for you, with nothing to plan or grade.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Abeka?
questions.answer: Abeka teaches math in daily lessons, in a fixed order for each grade, and the adult grades the work against answer keys [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Abeka work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Abeka's math. We found no Abeka entry in Evidence for ESSA, and the What Works Clearinghouse's only Abeka report, on early childhood in 2005, found no studies that met its standards [9][10].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. A family can keep Abeka's books or video lessons and use AMP for daily practice. AMP places a learner from their first answers, so it does not need to know where they are in the book.
